preamble: Glide formation turns the close back rounded vowel [u] into the labio-velar approximant [w] before another vowel. Between Classical Latin and Proto-Romance, unstressed back vowels in hiatus became /w/ (sapuī > /ˈsapwiː/), and so did stressed ones in the antepenult, with the stress moving to the preceding syllable (tenueram > /ˈtenwera/). French has the same process synchronically and optionally: an underlying high vowel becomes a glide before another vowel, so that loue [lu] alternates with louer [lwe] (Wiktionary also gives unglided /lu.e/), but usually not after an obstruent + liquid onset (clouer [klu.e]).

examples.from: Latin sapuī /ˈsapuiː/ 'I knew, I tasted of' (perfect of sapiō)
Latin tenueram /teˈnueram/ 'I had held' (pluperfect of teneō)
examples.note: The stressed u of the antepenult also became /w/, and the stress moved to the preceding syllable; final -m was lost as well.

languageExamples.context: Before a vowel, optionally (Wiktionary also gives unglided /lu.e/, /ʒu.e/); usually not after an obstruent + liquid onset

examples.note: After an obstruent + liquid onset the vowel stays syllabic: cloue [klu], clouer [klu.e] 'to nail'.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Phonological changes from Classical Latin to Proto-Romance. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonological_changes_from_Classical_Latin_to_Proto-Romance
